extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature/philosophy (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing or interpreting reflective, personal philosophical essays in the style of Montaigne—emphasizing moderation, first‑hand observation, and self‑examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The extremity of philosophy is hurtful, and advises not to dive into it beyond the limits of profit; that, taken moderately, it is pleasant and useful; but that in the end it renders a man brutish and vicious…” (Callicles in Plato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical inquiry should be kept within useful bounds: taken moderately it delights and benefits; in excess it alienates a person from religion, law, social life, and public usefulness. Avoid extremes—‘the archer that shoots over, misses as much as he that falls short.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control and temperate private pleasures (marriage/sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Marriage is a solemn and religious tie, and therefore the pleasure we extract from it should be a sober and serious delight, and mixed with a certain kind of gravity; it should be a sort of discreet and conscientious pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private pleasures—including conjugal relations—ought to be moderated and governed by duty and purpose (generation, solemnity). Immoderate or licentious behavior is reproachable; local religious and moral prescriptions that curb excess are defensible when they preserve reason and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report only what you know; prefer simple eyewitnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would have every one write what he knows, and as much as he knows, but no more.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value plain, direct testimony over embellished or learned glosses. Beware of ‘better‑bred’ or learned tellers who ‘gloss upon’ and alter stories to make themselves appear judicious. When recounting events or describing peoples, rely on first‑hand observation or consistent corroborating witnesses rather than speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by reason and observation, not by common report
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are to judge by the eye of reason, and not from common report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question received opinions and popular prejudices. Use critical observation and reasoned assessment (illustrated by Greeks misjudging Romans and vice versa) rather than accepting vulgar or traditional labels uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethnocentrism; question the label 'barbarous'
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call unfamiliar customs ‘barbarous’ simply because they differ. Recognize that what is ‘natural’ in one place may be degenerate or art‑adjusted in another; value native simplicity and virtues rather than assuming superiority based on local artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor remedies and penances so they have real effect
rubrics_metrics.description: On penances and punishments: the bitterness of the potion and the abhorrence of the patient are necessary circumstances to the operation; punishments should be real and affective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prescribing corrective action (moral, social, or medical), ensure the remedy produces the intended corrective experience. Avoid ceremonial or nominal penalties that fail to move or reform the subject (Gallio’s exile turning into pleasure is cited as a failed penance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold claimants of extraordinary faculties accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Divination is a gift of God, and therefore to abuse it, ought to be a punishable imposture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who assert supernatural or extraordinary powers (prophecy/divination) should be held to account when their predictions fail. The text gives violent historical examples of societies that punish false prophets—used to argue imposture merits sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose hypocrisy: compare others' cruelty with our own
rubrics_metrics.description: Although certain peoples practise cannibalism as ritual revenge, ‘we are ... blind to our own’ cruelties—tortures, racks, roasting alive—which may exceed those we condemn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral criticism of others should be accompanied by self‑examination; avoid hypocritically condemning ‘barbarity’ abroad while tolerating or practising cruelties at home. Use comparative examples to test moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define valour by inner courage rather than external advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: “The estimate and value of a man consist in the heart and in the will: there his true honour lies. Valour is stability, not of legs and arms, but of the courage and the soul; it does not lie in the goodness of our horse or our arms but in our own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bravery by constancy and moral courage, not by material equipment, numbers, or fortunate circumstances. Examples (Leonidas at Thermopylae, other heroic defeats) show defeat can still exemplify truest valor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor is in the encounter/fighting, not merely in victory
rubrics_metrics.description: “The part that true conquering is to play, lies in the encounter, not in the coming off; and the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure honour by willingness to face danger and uphold duty rather than by success or spoils. Some defeats (e.g., Thermopylae) are more glorious than many victories; the moral quality of resistance matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify origins: nature, fortune, or art
rubrics_metrics.description: “All things ... are produced either by nature, by fortune, or by art; the greatest and most beautiful by the one or the other of the former, the least and the most imperfect by the last.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating products, institutions, or customs, consider whether they derive from natural endowment, chance (fortune), or human artifice. Privilege what arises from nature or felicitous fortune over contrived artifice when judging purity, beauty, or authenticity.
